newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian regional currencies keep close eye on baht.
newsitem.headline: Asian regional currencies keep close eye on baht.

text.p: A firmer dollar in the wake of the Denver G7 meeting put some pressure on Asian region currencies on Monday, but the focus remained firmly on the baht as traders picked over the bones of the latest political and economic news from Thailand.

While the baht picked up quite strongly in European/U.S. trading on Friday there is still a huge amount of uncertainity -- not least about the credentials of the new finance minister Thanong Bidaya -- as Thailand remains mired in its worst economic slump for more than a decade.
Traders said as long as the Thai central bank holds onto its no-devaluation policy the baht is a lucrative, if somewhat dangerous, yield play.

In Asia today the offshore baht was trading around the 24.300/500 per US dollar level compared with 25.000/300 at the end of last week. The onshore baht was at 26.000/100, pretty much unchanged from Friday's level.
Around the region traders were monitoring the situation closely as further baht slippage, whether offically sanctioned or not, would have a knock-on impact on regional currencies.
"Whether justified or not, people would be very nervous about the other currencies," said Angus Armstrong, chief economist, Asia at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Economists said the Philippine peso would be the most obvious target because of the economic similiarites with Thailand, but the offshore peso market is too illiquid for speculative plays of any size.
The Indonesian rupiah is also a possible target as it has a fairly liquid and unregulated market but by past performance traders and analysts this it is reasonably safe.

"Taking a look at the rupiah's fairly steady performance during the baht crisis in May, you have to think that it won't be hurt that much by another," said one regional currency trader here. "Sure it's vulnerable but not as much as the ringgit."
It is certainly the Malaysian ringgit that is seen as the most exposed to a fresh baht slide -- it has the most liquidity with the best developed derivatives market.

"Whenever you have a currency in trouble you get a knock-on effect which has nothing to do with fundamentals. The ringgit is most at risk but we just think it would be a short period of instability, not to play it down, but we don't think any other
country in the region is in anything like the same position as Thailand," Deutsche's Armstrong said.

There are plenty of economic numbers out of Thailand this week for the market to peruse with reserves probably the most interesting to forex traders given the Bank of Thailand's efforts to shore-up the baht during the mid-May crisis.
The market is expecting a fall of around US$2.5 billion in May from April's US$37.3 billion. The April figure was down from March's US$38.1.

"This reserves figure will be extremely interesting and tell us something about what they (The Bank of Thailand) were up to in terms of the baht during May," one analyst at a North American bank said. "It's very difficult if not impossible to put a figure on it but most people seem to be going for around US$2.5 billion off."
Other data due from Thailand this week includes trade and current account data, manufacturing production figures and the private investment index, analysts said.
